title: Mass and Charge Transport Modeling, Multiphysics Analysis, and Architectural Optimization in Electrochemical Batteries: A Comprehensive Review
content: The rapid escalation of global decarbonization demands electrochemical energy storage systems that balance high energy density, superior rate capability, and decadal operational reliability. However, academic research has disproportionately focused on cell-level "specific capacity" records under idealized laboratory testing, obscuring the decisive governing role of macroscopic mass and charge transport architectures during scale-up. In this review, we formulate an interpretable physical framework that systematically classifies electrochemical batteries into four fundamental transport architectures: (1) enclosed stacked architectures, (2) Pure Liquid-Flow architectures, (3) fuel cells with the continuous-flow electrocatalytic reactor architectures, and (4) cross-phase hybrid architectures. We comprehensively evaluate how transport boundary conditions dictate electrochemical performance across the representative stacked systems (including high-nickel ternary, LMFP, solid-state, sodium-ion, aqueous zinc, and dual-ion batteries) and the true flow systems (ranging from all-vanadium, all-iron, polysulfide-iodide, to aqueous organic redox chemistries). Furthermore, we provide a unified taxonomy of hybrid systems spanning gas–solid (metal–air), liquid–solid (zinc–bromine, zinc–iodine, slurry flow), and gas–liquid (hydrogen–halogen, hydrogen–iron) configurations, explicitly demonstrating why hybrid configurations that superficially stitch disparate features inevitably inherit the transport liabilities and interfacial failure modes of both constituent architectures. Most critically, to address the core scope of battery performance modeling, we introduce a rigorous four-level multiphysics modeling framework spanning: (Level 1) geometric effective transport and through-plane ohmic resistance scaling, establishing a transparent and fully reproducible 35 mV IR-scale baseline for 100 μm thick electrodes; (Level 2) transient solid-state diffusion truncation and Sand's time interfacial electrodeposition instability modeling, physically justifying the ~10 mA cm-2 rate ceiling in high-loading stacked cells; (Level 3) hydrodynamic convective mass transfer and parasitic shunt-current network modeling in flow manifolds; and (Level 4) multiphase reaction-diffusion and electrocrystallization coupling dynamics. By bridging microscopic pore-scale transport dynamics and system-level architectural modeling, this review provides a quantitative roadmap for diagnosing transport limitations and guiding the rational design of scalable electrochemical batteries.
